result: Cep78 knockout mice exhibit progressive photoreceptor dysfunction and degeneration, characterized by reduced ERG amplitudes across scotopic and photopic conditions, impaired cone arrestin translocation, thinning of the outer nuclear layer, and disorganized photoreceptor outer segment structures.
evaluation: Claims C2-C8 provide comprehensive functional (ERG) and morphological (SD-OCT, TEM, immunofluorescence) evidence demonstrating photoreceptor impairment in Cep78−/− mice. The data show age-dependent progression with quantified measurements at multiple time points (3, 6, 9, 18 months) and appropriate controls (Cep78+/−). Statistical significance is reported, and multiple complementary techniques converge on the same conclusion.

result: Cep78 deficiency causes shortened connecting cilia with structural abnormalities in photoreceptors, including swelling and disorganized microtubules, while basal bodies and other inner segment organelles remain normal.
evaluation: Claims C9-C11 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data (Figure 2B) showing significant reduction in connecting cilium length at multiple ages, and TEM data (Figure 2E-G) revealing specific ultrastructural defects. The specificity of the defect is demonstrated by the preservation of basal body and other organelle structures.

result: Cep78 deletion causes complete male infertility in mice, associated with severely reduced sperm concentration, motility, and progressive motility, along with high percentages of morphologically abnormal sperm and dysregulated expression of proteins involved in sperm structure and function.
evaluation: Claims C12-C16 are supported by mating tests showing zero fertility (Figure 3A), CASA data demonstrating significant reductions in sperm parameters (Table 1), morphological analyses showing >90% abnormalities (Table 1), and mass spectrometry identifying 806 downregulated and 80 upregulated proteins with GO enrichment in relevant cellular components (Figure 3N-O).

result: Cep78−/− mice exhibit defective sperm flagella formation during spermatogenesis, characterized by disorganized mitochondria, deranged outer dense fibers, scattered 9+2 microtubules, ectopic triplet microtubules in middle and principal pieces, and elongated centrioles.
evaluation: Claims C17-C21 are supported by PAS staining showing flagellar defects at specific spermatogenesis stages (Figure 4A-B), TEM revealing ultrastructural abnormalities including the novel finding of triplet microtubules in abnormal locations (Figure 4E-J), and immunofluorescence demonstrating centriole elongation (Figure 4K). The data are internally consistent and use multiple complementary techniques.

result: Cep78−/− mice show abnormal spermatid head formation with club-shaped nuclei and defective manchette structures, including abnormal perinuclear rings and disordered manchette microtubules, while nuclear condensation and meiotic progression remain normal.
evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are supported by PAS staining (Figures 4B, 5A), immunofluorescence (Figure 5B), and TEM (Figure 5D-M) showing specific manchette and acrosome defects. The specificity is demonstrated by normal nuclear condensation (Figure 5N) and normal spermatocyte development through meiosis (Figure 5O-P), indicating the defect is specific to spermiogenesis.

result: A human patient carrying the CEP78 c.1629−2A>G mutation, which leads to loss of CEP78 protein, exhibits infertility with MMAF phenotypes highly similar to those observed in Cep78−/− mice, including reduced sperm parameters, high percentages of abnormal sperm, and ectopic triplet microtubules.
evaluation: Claims C27-C32 are supported by Western blot showing absence of CEP78 protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), CASA data showing reduced sperm parameters (Table 1), morphological analyses showing >95% abnormalities (Table 1, Figure 6A-J), and TEM revealing ultrastructural defects including the same ectopic triplet microtubules observed in mice (Figure 6K-R). The consistency between human and mouse phenotypes strengthens both findings.

result: CEP78 physically interacts with IFT proteins IFT20 and TTC21A, forming a protein complex, and is essential for the interaction between IFT20 and TTC21A, as demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation, size exclusion chromatography, and 3D-SIM localization studies.
evaluation: Claims C34-C39 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: IP-MS identifying 16 ciliary proteins including IFT20 and TTC21A (Table 2), co-IP experiments demonstrating pairwise interactions (Figure 7A-C), co-IP showing disrupted IFT20-TTC21A interaction in Cep78−/− mice (Figure 7D), size exclusion chromatography showing co-fractionation (Figure 7E), and 3D-SIM revealing spatial organization at the centriole (Figure 7F). The use of appropriate negative controls (Ap80-NB) strengthens the findings.

result: CEP78 regulates the stability and centriolar localization of IFT20 and TTC21A, with CEP78 loss leading to reduced levels of both proteins, shortened cilia, and elongated centrioles; knockdown of CEP78 or IFT20 (but not TTC21A) causes centriole elongation, while knockdown of any of the three proteins shortens cilia.
evaluation: Claims C40-C47 are supported by Western blots showing reduced IFT20 and TTC21A levels in Cep78−/− testes and Cep78-siRNA cells (Figure 7G-M), immunofluorescence showing shortened cilia after knockdown of any protein (Figure 7N-O), centriole elongation after Cep78 or IFT20 but not TTC21A knockdown (Figure 7P-Q), and disrupted IFT20 localization after Cep78 knockdown (Figure 7R-S). The asymmetry (CEP78 affects IFT20/TTC21A but not vice versa) supports a hierarchical relationship. Rescue experiments with synonymous mutants strengthen the specificity of the findings.

result: CEP78 is a 722 amino acid centriolar protein with leucine-rich repeats and a coiled-coil domain, localizing to the distal region of mature centrioles, exclusively expressed in ciliated organisms, and mutations cause autosomal recessive CRDHL and other diseases.
evaluation: Claims C48-C53 are supported by multiple citations to established literature (Brunk et al., 2016; Hossain, 2017; Azimzadeh et al., 2012; Fu, 2017; Nikopoulos et al., 2016; Namburi et al., 2016; Sanchis-Juan et al., 2018; Ascari et al., 2020; Gonçalves et al., 2021). These are well-established facts about CEP78 structure, localization, and disease associations that provide appropriate context for the study.

result: IFT20 and TTC21A are IFT proteins (IFT-B and IFT-A subcomplexes, respectively) that interact with each other and are essential for spermatogenesis, ciliogenesis, and sperm flagella formation, with mutations causing MMAF in both humans and mice.
evaluation: Claims C54-C67 and C98-C113 are supported by multiple citations to established literature (Liu et al., 2019; Petriman et al., 2022; Hesketh et al., 2022; Keady et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2016a; Kazarian et al., 2018; Hibbard et al., 2021; Wingfield et al., 2021). These provide appropriate background on IFT proteins and their known functions, contextualizing the novel findings about CEP78's interaction with these proteins.

result: Background on ciliopathies, CRD syndromes, manchette structure, and previous CEP78 studies establishes the context and novelty of the current findings, including the unprecedented observation of ectopic triplet microtubules in sperm flagella.
evaluation: Claims C58-C109 provide appropriate background information supported by citations to relevant literature (Zhu et al., 2002; Kubota et al., 2018; Yıldız Bölükbaşı et al., 2018; Gill et al., 2019; Khanna et al., 2005; Kierszenbaum and Tres, 2004; Lehti and Sironen, 2016; Kierszenbaum et al., 2002; Akhmanova et al., 2005; Kierszenbaum et al., 2011; Karlstetter et al., 2014; Avidor-Reiss and Fishman, 2019; Gonçalves et al., 2021). These claims establish the knowledge gaps and novelty of the findings, particularly the unprecedented observation of triplet microtubules in abnormal locations.

result: The study establishes CEP78 as a causative gene for CRD and male infertility syndrome, with Cep78−/− mice serving as an applicable animal model due to high conservation between human and mouse CEP78 and consistent phenotypes, providing a basis for molecular diagnosis and potential gene therapy.
evaluation: Claims C68, C77, C115-C116, and C119-C121 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the comprehensive data showing consistent phenotypes between human patient and mouse model. The claim about >80% similarity between human and mouse CEP78 is verifiable. However, claims C120-C121 about molecular diagnosis and gene therapy are somewhat speculative, as no diagnostic or therapeutic interventions were actually tested. These represent potential applications rather than demonstrated results.

result: CEP78 may regulate sperm flagellum formation through a different mechanism than CP110, as CEP78 loss leads to shortened flagella with downregulated CP110, contrasting with previous findings in cell culture showing upregulated CP110 and long cilia.
evaluation: Claims C74-C75 are based on the observation that CP110 is downregulated in Cep78−/− testes (Figure 7—figure supplement 5), which contrasts with Gonçalves et al., 2021's findings in cell culture. However, the mechanistic interpretation is speculative. The difference could reflect tissue-specific regulation, developmental context, or differences between primary cilia and sperm flagella rather than a fundamentally different mechanism. Additional experiments would be needed to establish the proposed different mechanism.
